question_text: Which star is at the center of our Solar System?
column9: The Sun is the G-type main-sequence star around which all planetary bodies in our Solar System orbit.

question_text: How many confirmed major planets are there in our Solar System?
column9: Following the 2006 IAU reclassification of Pluto there are 8 recognized major planets.

question_text: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
column9: Mercury is the innermost planet with an orbital period of roughly 88 Earth days.

question_text: Which planet is the hottest in our Solar System due to a runaway greenhouse effect?
column9: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat creating surface temperatures over 460°C.

question_text: What is the largest planet in our Solar System?
column9: Jupiter is a gas giant with more mass than all other planets combined.

question_text: Which planet is known for its prominent bright planetary ring system visible from Earth?
column9: Saturn has the most extensive and visually prominent ring system composed of ice and rock particles.

question_text: Which planet is nicknamed the 'Red Planet' because of iron oxide on its surface?
column9: Mars appears reddish to observers due to pervasive iron oxide (rust) dust covering its crust.

question_text: Which planet is famous for rotating on its side with an axial tilt of nearly 98 degrees?
column9: Uranus has an extreme axial tilt of 97.8° causing it to rotate nearly parallel to its orbital plane.

question_text: What is the outermost recognized major planet from the Sun in our Solar System?
column9: Neptune is the eighth and farthest known major planet from the Sun.

question_text: What celestial classification was given to Pluto by the International Astronomical Union in 2006?
column9: The IAU classified Pluto as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its neighboring orbital region.

question_text: What is Earth's only permanent natural satellite?
column9: The Moon is Earth's sole permanent natural satellite orbiting at an average distance of ~384 400 km.

question_text: How long does it take for Earth to complete one full orbit around the Sun?
column9: Earth completes one revolution around the Sun in approximately 365.25 days defining one calendar year.

question_text: What causes the cycle of day and night on Earth?
column9: Earth rotates once on its axis every 24 hours exposing different hemispheres to solar light.

question_text: What causes the changing seasons on Earth throughout the year?
column9: Earth's 23.5° axial tilt alters the angle and duration of solar insolation received as Earth orbits the Sun.

question_text: What gravitational interaction primarily drives ocean tides on Earth?
column9: Tidal bulges are primarily generated by the differential gravitational attraction of the Moon.

question_text: What astronomical event occurs when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth?
column9: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon casts its shadow onto Earth obscuring the solar disk.

question_text: What astronomical event occurs when Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon?
column9: A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the full Moon casting Earth's umbral shadow.

question_text: Why does the same side of the Moon always face Earth?
column9: Tidal friction has locked the Moon's rotation period to match its orbital period around Earth exactly.

question_text: What are the dark flat basaltic plains on the Moon called?
column9: Early astronomers mistook these dark volcanic basalt basins for liquid oceans naming them 'maria' (seas).

question_text: What is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun?
column10: 1 Astronomical Unit (AU) is approximately 149.6 million kilometers.

question_text: Which is the largest moon in the entire Solar System orbiting Jupiter?
column9: Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.

question_text: Which moon of Saturn has a dense nitrogen atmosphere and liquid methane lakes on its surface?
column9: Titan has a dense orange nitrogen-rich atmosphere and active hydrological cycles driven by liquid hydrocarbons.

question_text: Which Galilean moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System?
column9: Io experiences extreme tidal heating from Jupiter driving over 400 active sulfurous volcanoes.

question_text: Which ice-covered moon of Jupiter is believed to harbor a vast subsurface liquid water ocean beneath its crust?
column9: Europa's smooth cracked icy surface conceals a global saltwater ocean that may harbor conditions for life.

question_text: What are the two small irregularly shaped natural satellites orbiting Mars?
column9: Mars possesses two small captured asteroid-like moons named Phobos and Deimos.

question_text: Which icy moon of Saturn shoots plumes of water vapor and ice grains into space from south polar fractures?
column9: Enceladus vents subsurface ocean water through 'tiger stripe' geysers feeding Saturn's E-ring.

question_text: Which moon of Neptune orbits in a retrograde direction (opposite to the planet's rotation)?
column9: Triton is a captured Kuiper Belt dwarf planet and the only large moon in the Solar System with a retrograde orbit.

question_text: Which moon resembles the fictional 'Death Star' due to the massive Herschel impact crater on its surface?
column9: Saturn's moon Mimas features the 130-kilometer-wide Herschel impact crater.

question_text: Which is the largest moon of the dwarf planet Pluto?
column9: Charon is so massive relative to Pluto that the two orbit a shared barycenter situated outside Pluto's surface.

question_text: Which moon of Uranus features chaotic fractured terrain with massive cliff faces named Verona Rupes?
column9: Miranda displays extreme geologic disruption including the tallest known cliff in the Solar System (Verona Rupes).

question_text: What nuclear fusion process powers main-sequence stars like our Sun?
column9: Stars generate radiative energy by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium within their high-pressure cores.

question_text: What color are the hottest main-sequence stars in the universe?
column9: Blue stars have surface temperatures exceeding 20 000 K radiating peak energy in ultraviolet and blue wavelengths.

question_text: What color are the coolest visible stars?
column9: Red stars have surface temperatures around 2 500 to 3 500 K.

question_text: What massive stellar explosion marks the destructive end of a high-mass star's life cycle?
column9: A supernova is a catastrophic explosion that disperses heavy synthesized elements into interstellar space.

question_text: What dense stellar remnant is left behind after a low-to-medium mass star like our Sun exhausts its fuel?
column9: Our Sun will shed its outer envelope as a planetary nebula leaving behind an electron-degenerate white dwarf core.

question_text: What extremely dense celestial object is formed when a massive star collapses leaving gravity so strong that not even light can escape?
column9: A black hole forms when mass collapses within its Schwarzschild radius creating an inescapable gravitational event horizon.

question_text: What type of star is commonly called a 'failed star' because it lacks the mass needed to sustain hydrogen fusion?
column9: Brown dwarfs have masses between 13 and 80 Jupiter masses allowing deuterium fusion but not stable hydrogen burning.

question_text: What is the name of the bright North Star used for navigation in the Northern Hemisphere?
column9: Polaris aligns closely with Earth's northern rotational axis in the constellation Ursa Minor.

question_text: Which star is the brightest individual star in the night sky as viewed from Earth?
column9: Sirius in Canis Major has an apparent visual magnitude of -1.46 making it the brightest star in Earth's sky.

question_text: What is the closest star system to our Solar System located roughly 4.24 light-years away?
column9: The Alpha Centauri system (featuring Proxima Centauri) is the nearest stellar neighbor to our Sun.

question_text: What is a vast gravitationally bound system of stars stellar remnants gas and dark matter called?
column9: A galaxy is a massive cosmic structure containing millions to trillions of stars bound by mutual gravity.

question_text: What type of galaxy is our Milky Way Galaxy classified as?
column9: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with a central stellar bar and sweeping spiral arms.

question_text: What supermassive black hole sits at the gravitational center of the Milky Way galaxy?
column9: Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole with a mass of roughly 4.1 million solar masses.

question_text: What is the nearest major spiral galaxy to the Milky Way located about 2.5 million light-years away?
column9: The Andromeda Galaxy is the largest neighboring galaxy in the Local Group and is on a collision course with the Milky Way.

question_text: What prevailing scientific theory explains the expansion of the universe from a hot dense initial singularity?
column9: The Big Bang theory is the standard cosmological model describing the origin and expansion of the cosmos ~13.8 billion years ago.

question_text: What distance unit represents the distance that light travels through a vacuum in one Earth year?
column9: One light-year equals approximately 9.46 trillion kilometers (5.88 trillion miles).

question_text: What vast interstellar clouds of gas and dust serve as the stellar nurseries where new stars are born?
column9: Nebulae (such as the Orion Nebula) collapse gravitationally to form protostars and planetary systems.

question_text: What pattern of recognizable stars in the night sky is officially mapped into 88 modern regions by the IAU?
column9: The IAU officially divides the celestial sphere into 88 recognized constellations.

question_text: What famous asterism forms part of the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear)?
column9: The Big Dipper is an easily recognized seven-star asterism within the larger Ursa Major constellation.

question_text: What mysterious invisible form of matter is believed to make up roughly 85% of all matter in the universe?
column9: Dark matter does not absorb or emit electromagnetic radiation interacting primarily through gravitational effects.

question_text: Where is the Main Asteroid Belt located in our Solar System?
column9: The Main Asteroid Belt resides in the interplanetary gap separating the rocky inner planets from the gas giants.

question_text: What is the largest object in the Main Asteroid Belt classified as both an asteroid and a dwarf planet?
column9: Ceres contains about a third of the total mass in the asteroid belt and is round under its own gravity.

question_text: What celestial object made of ice dust and rock develops a glowing coma and tails when approaching the Sun?
column9: Cometary ice sublimates when heated by the Sun creating gaseous envelopes and sweeping ion/dust tails.

question_text: What is a small rocky or metallic body traveling through interplanetary space before hitting an atmosphere called?
column9: A meteoroid is small debris in space; when it burns in an atmosphere it is a meteor and if it lands it is a meteorite.

question_text: What is the streak of light produced when space debris vaporizes upon entering Earth's atmosphere called?
column9: Meteors produce radiant streaks of ionized air and burning debris colloquially called shooting stars.

question_text: What is a fragment of extraterrestrial rock that survives passage through the atmosphere and strikes the Earth's surface called?
column9: Meteorites are surviving physical specimens collected on the ground (stony iron or stony-iron).

question_text: What famous periodic comet returns to the inner Solar System and is visible from Earth approximately every 75 to 76 years?
column9: Halley's Comet was last observed in 1986 and will return to perihelion in mid-2061.

question_text: What vast reservoir of icy bodies and dwarf planets extends beyond the orbit of Neptune (from 30 to 50 AU)?
column9: The Kuiper Belt contains millions of primitive icy planetesimals including Pluto Haumea and Makemake.

question_text: What theoretical spherical cloud of trillions of icy cometary bodies surrounds the outer boundary of the Solar System up to 100 000 AU?
column9: The Oort Cloud is the hypothesized distant source of long-period comets surrounding the Solar System.

question_text: What annual meteor shower peaks in mid-August when Earth passes through debris left by Comet Swift-Tuttle?
column9: The Perseid meteor shower is one of the brightest annual showers radiant from the constellation Perseus.

question_text: What was the name of the first artificial satellite launched into Earth orbit by the Soviet Union in October 1957?
column9: Sputnik 1 was launched on October 4 1957 initiating the Space Age and Space Race.

question_text: Who was the first human being to travel into space and orbit Earth in April 1961?
column9: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth aboard Vostok 1 on April 12 1961.

question_text: Who was the first American astronaut to travel into space in May 1961 aboard Freedom 7?
column9: Alan Shepard completed a suborbital spaceflight on May 5 1961.

question_text: Which NASA Apollo mission successfully landed the first humans on the Moon in July 1969?
column9: Apollo 11 landed astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the lunar surface on July 20 1969.

question_text: What was the name of the lunar module that landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon?
column9: The Apollo 11 Lunar Module was named 'Eagle' ('The Eagle has landed').

question_text: Who was the first woman to fly in space aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963?
column9: Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova completed 48 orbits of Earth during her historic solo mission.

question_text: Who was the first American woman to travel into space launching aboard Space Shuttle Challenger in 1983?
column9: Dr. Sally Ride flew into space aboard STS-7 in June 1983.

question_text: What habitable artificial satellite has been continuously occupied by international astronaut crews in Low Earth Orbit since November 2000?
column9: The ISS represents a joint partnership between NASA Roscosmos ESA JAXA and CSA.

question_text: What legendary space telescope launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and transformed observational astronomy?
column9: The Hubble Space Telescope has operated for decades providing deep-field optical views of the cosmos.

question_text: What next-generation infrared space observatory launched on Christmas Day 2021 to observe the earliest galaxies?
column9: JWST operates around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point capturing infrared views of high-redshift early galaxies.

question_text: What NASA robotic rover successfully landed inside Jezero Crater on Mars in February 2021 carrying the Ingenuity helicopter?
column9: Perseverance explores Jezero Crater seeking biosignatures and caching rock core samples for return.

question_text: What was the name of the first robotic rotorcraft/helicopter to achieve powered controlled flight on another planet (Mars)?
column9: NASA's Ingenuity Mars Helicopter completed 72 flights on Mars proving aerodynamic flight in thin atmospheres.

question_text: Which twin NASA space probes launched in 1977 explored the outer gas giants and have both entered interstellar space?
column9: Voyager 1 and 2 performed grand tours of the outer planets and continue transmitting data from beyond the heliopause.

question_text: Which robotic spacecraft performed the first historic flyby of Pluto and its moons in July 2015?
column9: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft captured high-resolution images of Pluto's nitrogen ice plains and mountains.

question_text: Which NASA spacecraft orbited and explored Saturn its majestic rings and moons from 2004 until plunging into its atmosphere in 2017?
column9: The Cassini mission discovered subsurface oceans on Enceladus and methane weather on Titan.

question_text: What was the name of the European Space Agency lander that touched down on Saturn's moon Titan in January 2005?
column9: The ESA Huygens probe descended through Titan's atmosphere landing on a surface smoothed by liquid methane flows.

question_text: What European Space Agency spacecraft landed the Philae probe on Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014?
column9: Rosetta was the first mission to rendezvous with and escort a comet deploying the Philae lander.

question_text: What spacecraft launched by NASA in 2011 has been orbiting Jupiter to investigate its internal magnetic and gravitational fields?
column9: Juno orbits Jupiter in a polar trajectory analyzing water abundance core structure and magnetosphere dynamics.

question_text: What NASA spacecraft impacted the asteroid moon Dimorphos in 2022 to successfully demonstrate planetary defense kinetic redirection?
column9: DART altered the orbital period of Dimorphos around Didymos by 33 minutes verifying kinetic deflection capabilities.

question_text: Which NASA mission collected pristine asteroid regolith samples from Bennu and successfully returned them to Earth in September 2023?
column9: OSIRIS-REx delivered carbon-rich asteroid samples from 101955 Bennu to the Utah desert in 2023.

question_text: What colorful natural light display occurs in high-latitude skies when solar charged particles interact with Earth's upper atmosphere?
column9: Auroras are caused by solar wind particles guided along magnetic field lines exciting nitrogen and oxygen atoms in the ionosphere.

question_text: What is the northern light display called in the Northern Hemisphere?
column9: The northern lights are formally termed the Aurora Borealis while southern lights are Aurora Australis.

question_text: What is the temporary dark relatively cool region on the Sun's photosphere caused by concentrated magnetic fields called?
column9: Sunspots appear darker because their intense magnetic fields inhibit convective heat flow lowering localized temperature.

question_text: What explosive burst of electromagnetic radiation and energetic particles erupts from the solar atmosphere near sunspots?
column9: Solar flares release stored magnetic energy accelerating electrons and protons across interplanetary space.

question_text: What continuous stream of charged particles (electrons and protons) flows outward from the Sun throughout the Solar System?
column9: The solar wind flows outward past Pluto creating the protective magnetic bubble known as the heliosphere.

question_text: What optical telescope type uses curved glass lenses to collect and bend light to form an image?
column9: Refractors utilize convex glass objective lenses to focus incoming light rays onto an eyepiece.

question_text: What optical telescope type uses a curved primary mirror to gather and focus light invented by Sir Isaac Newton?
column9: Newtonian reflectors use concave parabolic mirrors to eliminate chromatic aberration found in early lens refractors.

question_text: What is the boundary or imaginary dome where the sky appears to meet the Earth's surface called?
column9: The horizon is the apparent line that separates earth from sky for an observer.

question_text: What is the imaginary point on the celestial sphere directly above an observer's head called?
column9: The zenith is the point with an altitude of +90 degrees pointing directly overhead.

question_text: What is the point on the celestial sphere directly beneath an observer's feet called?
column9: The nadir is the point diametrically opposite to the zenith pointing straight downward.

question_text: Which commercial space company founded by Elon Musk developed the reusable Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon spacecraft?
column9: SpaceX pioneered orbital rocket first-stage propulsive landings and commercial astronaut transport.

question_text: What is the name of NASA's modern lunar exploration program aiming to return humans to the Moon and establish a sustainable base?
column9: The Artemis program utilizes the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion spacecraft for crewed lunar exploration.

question_text: What is the minimum speed an object must achieve to break free from Earth's gravitational pull without further propulsion?
column9: Earth's escape velocity from its surface is approximately 11.2 km/s (roughly 25 000 mph).

question_text: What state of apparent weightlessness is experienced by astronauts orbiting Earth in free fall?
column9: Orbital spacecraft are in constant free fall around Earth producing continuous microgravity conditions.

question_text: What is a celestial planet that orbits a star outside our Solar System called?
column9: Exoplanets orbit distant stars throughout the galaxy with thousands confirmed by missions like Kepler and TESS.

question_text: What space telescope launched by NASA in 2009 discovered thousands of transiting exoplanets?
column9: Kepler monitored the slight periodic dimming of distant stars as exoplanets crossed in front of their stellar disks.

question_text: What is a planet that has been ejected from its parent star system and wanders interstellar space called?
column9: Rogue planets drift through interstellar space without being gravitationally bound to any host star.

question_text: What zone around a star allows liquid water to exist on a planetary surface without boiling or freezing?
column9: The circumstellar habitable zone defines orbital distances where stellar irradiation permits liquid surface water.

question_text: What groundbreaking international telescope collaboration produced the first direct silhouette image of a black hole in 2019?
column9: The EHT linked global radio dishes via VLBI to image the shadow of the supermassive black hole M87*.

question_text: What is the approximate age of the universe according to modern Planck satellite cosmological measurements?
column9: Precise cosmic microwave background measurements date the origin of the universe to approximately 13.787 billion years.
